beliefs.practice: Create a single MongoClient instance and reuse it across the whole Node.js process (connect once at startup), set poolSize (maxPoolSize) appropriately (e.g. maxPoolSize: 50) and close it only on graceful shutdown.

Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) or a secrets store; do NOT commit credentials to the repo; prefer a managed secret store (Azure Key Vault) or environment-based provisioning for production.
Enable and use TLS/SSL for connections (ssl=true / tls=true) and restrict allowed client IPs via the cluster firewall; require certificates if supported and avoid plain-text connections.
Use a least-privilege database user/role for the app (separate write user for categorization writes and read-only user for analytics) rather than the cluster master key; rotate credentials regularly.
For monetary amounts, store as integer cents (or a fixed-point integer) and include an explicit currency field; avoid floating-point storage for amounts.
Store timestamps in UTC using an ISODate/Date type and use ISO 8601 strings only when necessary; use a date field named 'date' and index it for time-based queries/aggregations.

Create a compound index that supports the primary aggregation and filter patterns — e.g. an index { date: 1, category: 1 } (or { category: 1, date: 1 } depending on match patterns) to accelerate monthly-spend queries; use explain() to verify the index is used.

When you only need to categorize uncategorised transactions, use a partial index or a filtered index (partialFilterExpression: { category: { $exists: false } }) to speed scans of uncategorized documents.

Make categorization updates idempotent by using conditional updates (e.g. findOneAndUpdate filter { _id:..., category: { $exists: false } } and $set the category), and avoid blind re-writes so multiple runs won't reclassify or overwrite audited labels.

Batch transactions for LLM prompts: group multiple uncategorized transactions into a single prompt (size-limited) to reduce LLM calls and speed processing; process in bounded batch sizes (e.g. 10–50 documents) and persist results per-document.

Record the LLM prompt, model id, embeddings (if used), and model response (or a checksum) in a separate audit collection when categorizing documents so you can re-run or debug decisions later without re-querying user data.

Use the driver and cloud provider retry features: enable retryWrites/retryReads on the MongoDB driver, implement application-level retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors, and only retry idempotent operations automatically.

Use aggregation pipeline on the server (e.g. $group with $dateToString or $dateTrunc to bucket by month) for the monthly spend endpoint to avoid shipping large result sets to the app server; ensure the pipeline filters by date range and category before grouping.

If using embeddings or vector similarity for categorization helper lookups, store an embeddings field (e.g. 'embedding': [float,...]) and create the cluster's vector index with explicit parameters (indexType: 'hnsw' or 'ivf', M, efConstruction, metric: 'cosine' or 'dot'), and verify vector search syntax supported by this MongoDB-compatible API.

Avoid long-running transactions for categorization; use single-document atomic updates where possible and perform multi-document work as idempotent batches — if multi-document ACID is required, use the driver's transaction API but keep transactions short.
Seed scripts should be idempotent: use updateOne/upsert:true or bulkWrite with upsert and a unique key to avoid duplicate sample data; do not run seeds automatically in production environments.

Instrument queries with explain() and indexStats in development to confirm aggregation pipelines and indexes are used; capture RU/throughput metrics (or equivalent) to detect expensive queries, and optimize queries that perform COLLSCANs.

Protect PII before sending text to an external LLM: redact or hash personally-identifying fields (account numbers, full names) in the prompt or obtain explicit consent and document the data sent to the model.

Use server-side pagination (limit/skip or range-based using an indexed cursor) when reading many documents for batching; prefer range-based (e.g. _id or date) to avoid expensive skip on large collections.

For production throughput, prefer autoscale or provisioned RU/s appropriate to expected ingestion and LLM-driven write bursts; monitor RU consumption and add throttling/backpressure in the worker to avoid throttling errors.
When updating many documents from an agent run, use bulkWrite with ordered:false and handle partial failures; record which docs were updated and which failed so the run can be retried safely.

Limit the LLM model context by pre-formatting transaction data (concise templates) and include a fixed taxonomy in the prompt; validate that the model's output strictly matches one of the taxonomy values before writing to the DB.
Restrict your app's DB operations to the sample database 'sample_fintech_02' (set this in the client or in env) and avoid elevated privileges that can access other databases on the cluster.

Use explain('executionStats') or the provider's query profiler to detect expensive stages in aggregate pipelines (e.g. $group over large unfiltered sets) and add pre-filtering matches and appropriate indexes to reduce scanned documents.
